column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The entry says he gained Berat after 1355; the article says Berat belonged to his appanage from 1345 and that Stephen Uroš captured it in 1356. Berat is left out. The article says he 'probably' died of plague in 1363; the text keeps the hedge without contradicting the entry.
The entry gives his journey as about 900 km; the article says nearly 600 miles (970 km). The distance is left out.

The article says he left three sisters as co-heiresses but that Henry III bought the honour of Chester in 1246 from his four sisters; the 1246 sentence says only 'his sisters'. A short article (about 300 words); the text uses nearly all of it without padding.

The death toll of 64 is in the entry and the article attributes it to Vietnamese reports; it is not repeated. Cheng Tun-jen and Tien Hung-mao say seven reefs and rocks were taken within a year; the six by the end of 1988 is the article's main figure and is used.
The entry dates him c. 1790–1861; the article gives his birth as 3 February 1785. His birth date is left out. A short article (about 300 words); two sections only.

The article says Godoy named him viceroy 'after serving as governor of Cádiz from 1793 to 1798' and also that he commanded in the War of the Oranges in 1801; the text keeps the order without dating the appointment. The article puts the arrest on 15 September and his term as ending 16 September 1808; the entry says only September 1808.

The article says the Republic of Spanish Haiti lasted from 1 December 1821 to 9 February 1822; the entry says Haitian forces occupied the country in February 1822. Consistent; the day is not repeated. The article's account of his reopening of the university (1815, 6 January 1815) is used without the day.
The article says he captured Valencia and Caracas 'the following month' after La Puerta on 15 June 1814; written as July 1814.

The article gives the length of his address to the jury as more than six hours in its lead and more than five hours in its section on the trial; the length is left out. The article dates his resignation as Provincial Secretary to become railway commissioner to 1853 in one section and 1854 in another; no year is given.

The entry names Blue Jacket beside Little Turtle; the article names only Little Turtle for the defeat. Blue Jacket is not mentioned. The article calls his trial both a court-martial and a court of inquiry; written as a court of inquiry, which cleared him.

The entry dates the Higüey campaign to 1503–1504; the article says Ovando sent him in 1502, that Las Casas attributed a second expedition of 1504 to him, and that he was in Spain then (he was named procurador 'around 1504'). The campaign and the procurador mission are told without years; the second expedition is left out. The article says the region was pacified in 1505; left out with the other campaign dates.
The article calls him bishop 'from 1542' and says he was appointed in 1541 and accepted the election on 15 January 1542; the entry's 'elected in 1541' is kept by saying he was named in 1541.
The entry says Anzhou destroyed the kingdom of Jushi around 450; the article does not mention Jushi, so nothing is said of it. A short article (about 460 words); the text uses most of it.

The article's English rendering of the opening chant is loose (it mentions wolves and hell) and is not used; only the first line of the main body is translated. The article's sentence on the Kiwis ('until 2013, when Te Iwi Kiwi was used instead') is ambiguous about which team changed; the date is left out.

The article's claim that UNESCO has recognised them since 2004 is unclear in its sourcing and is left out. The genetic studies (mtDNA, Y-DNA) take up much of the article; left out as too technical for the space.

The article gives two meanings for the name: 'the ancestor, the one who was' (from Ka-Woon) and 'this is the one' (when Mbegane Ndour renamed the capital). Neither meaning is given. The article's rebuttal of Rokhaya Fall names the princess as Kina/Kin/Kon O Mev/Meo Mane (Manneh); left unnamed because of the many spellings. The entry calls the king Buur Saloum; the article speaks of the O Maad at the modern festival. Both kept to their own context.
The entry says Copán's king was sacrificed; the article says captured and later beheaded. Written as beheaded. A short article (about 350 words); two sections.
The article names the 19-syllable metre as Śardūlawikrīd[?]ita (a damaged character); the name is left out. A short article (about 500 words, much of it in the entry already); two sections.

The article dates the first castle to the Bunmei era (1469-1487); the entry says the early 16th century. Left out. The article says the castle was surrendered to the Tokugawa in 1568 by Asahina Yasutomo after a five-month siege; the entry says Imagawa Ujizane held out there and surrendered in 1569. The year and the name of who surrendered are left out.
The article is short; the entry's Sufi origins and canal building are not in it and are not repeated. The article's list of rulers is empty in the saved copy.

The article dates his death to 25 November 1466; the entry has d. 1467. No death date is given in the text. The article gives the coronation as 29 June 1435; the entry says he seized the throne in 1434. Left out. The article's figures for his army (200,000 elephants, 700,000 infantry) come from Muslim sources the article treats as inflated; left out.
The article gives no date for Cook's death; the entry's 14 February 1779 is not repeated. The article gives the ships' return as 12 February.

The article dates Hertford's destruction only to the 1540s; the entry's 1545 is not repeated. The article says the abbey was closed in 2022 over decaying stonework and re-opened in July 2026 after repairs.

The article says radiocarbon dates from Tell Abu Salabikh put the site at 2550-2520 BCE, slightly later than Biggs's c. 2600 BCE, which the entry follows. The radiocarbon figure is left out. The article gives 'around 145 lines' for Langdon's Ashmolean prism and 134 lines for the hymn; the text uses 134 for the hymn. Biggs's doubts about where Kesh lay (Abu Salabikh, near Adab, or a spelling of Kish) are left out.

The article gives his reign as 1418-1465 and his father Ibrahim I's as 1382-1418; the entry has 1417-1465. The accession year and Ibrahim's dates are left out. The article does not state why the body was desecrated in 1500; no motive is given in the text.
The article gives the four lines as Afrighids (305-995), Ma'munids (995-1017), Altuntash (1017-1041) and Anushteginids (1097-1231); consistent with the entry.
The article says the 'Loch Awe school' of carving is doubted by a 2010 reassessment; left out. Kilmartin Castle has been restored as a private house.

The article's opening gives his dates as 355-299 BC, but its own narrative has him die in captivity three years after his capture in 299 BC, i.e. in 296 BCE, as the entry says. Neither the birth year nor the 299 death date is used.
The article dates his reign from 515 BC; the entry has 516-489 BCE. The accession year is left out. The article does not give the year of his death; the entry's 489 BCE is not repeated.

The article says he paid homage to King John of Bohemia in 1328; the entry says 1329. Left out. The article's wording on Milicz ('bought Milicz to the Bishopric of Wrocław') is unclear; the text says only that he bought it.

The article gives the number of cars burned as both 80 and over seventy; the entry has around 80. No figure is used. The article has the riot begin in the early hours of 20 December and also on the night of 20 December into the next morning; the text gives no date beyond the entry's.
The article says the inscriptions were opened to the public on 4 May 1868, matching the entry's completion year.

The article says Adela Velarde Pérez 'fell in love with Madero'; left out as an unsupported aside. The article's sections on soldaderas also report that Zapatistas kidnapped and raped women from villages that fed them; left out as being about the revolution rather than the song.
President Egils Levits's 2021 message linking the day to the COVID-19 pandemic is left out.
The article names only 'Cortes'. The Pemex threats and the 'critically threatened' rating are left out under the rule on present-day assessments.

The article's lead gives the Ming relief force as 110,000 men, its body as 70,000 plus 45,200 = 115,200; no figure is printed. The article has a section 'Uprising in Lam Sơn (1416–1418)' for the preparations; the entry's start date 1418 is kept (the lead says the uprising began in early 1418).

The article is general and legal; it does not treat the Ottoman, Ethiopian, Darfur or Median systems the entry names. The text keeps to the historical parts and leaves out the present-day country rules and the section on modern housing.
The article gives his death as 437 BC without 'c.'; the entry has d. c. 437 BCE, so no year of death is printed.

The article says Juan Cabré researched the site in the 1920s; the entry's 'from 1927' is not contradicted, and no year is printed. The DNA samples come from other sites of the culture, not from Las Cogotas, and the text says so.

The article dates the building to 1375-1378; the entry says the 1370s or 1380s, so no building date is printed. The article gives the internal length as '15.65 feet (4.77 m)', an evident slip; left out.

The article puts Lê Hiển Tông's death and Lê Chiêu Thống's accession in 1787; the entry gives his reign as 1786 to 1789, so no accession year is printed. The article's lead says the Qianlong Emperor banished remaining Lê family members to Xinjiang and Heilongjiang, while the body says they were made banner officials and farmers in Sichuan and Zhejiang; the banishment is left out.

The article names the Song emperor who declined to invade as Taizong; Taizong had died before 1005, so the emperor is not named. The 1008 embassy is dated by the article to 'the 14th year of the Ứng Thiên era', an era name different from his own Cảnh Thụy; only the year 1008 is printed.
The article names Andreas Fromm (d. 1685) as the commonly believed forger, yet dates the text to 1688-1700; Fromm is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, much of it a list of attributed works

The article says the main group of about 200 was commanded by Tibor Szamuely and that Cserny led a separate militia often conflated with it; the entry says the Lenin Boys were led by Cserny and associated with Szamuely. The text names both without saying who commanded the group. The article's lead says Béla Kun used the 'Lenin Youth' after a coup attempt in June 1919; left out as unclear.

The article gives his birth as 1597 and says he became prince at fourteen; the entry gives 1591-1657, so neither birth year nor age is printed. The article has his sister Mariam marrying both Simon Gurieli and Rostom of Kartli; only the Rostom marriage of 1633 is printed. It also gives the mutilation of Tamunia differently in two places (ears and nose; nose, ears and tongue), so the text says only that she was mutilated.

The article reports that some historians (József Deér, Dezső Dümmerth, Jenő Szűcs, György Szabados) place Levedi in the 7th or 8th century, which would contradict the entry's '9th century'; these views are left out and only 9th-century datings are printed. The article notes that the story of the Hungarians leaving their homeland after a Pecheneg defeat in fact reflects a later Bulgar and Pecheneg counter-invasion; not printed.
The article dates his brother's reign to 1696-1697 or, more probably, 1701-1703; no accession year is printed.

The article says he died near the border between Yunnan and Laos; the entry says the borderlands of Yunnan and Burma, so no place of death is printed. The article gives 10 August 1662 in the lead and 'probably in August 1662' in the body; the lead's date matches the entry's year.

The article dates the Mongol Yamen to 1636 and its renaming as Lifan Yuan to 1639; the entry says founded in 1638. The article dates the change to the Lifan Ministry to 1907; the entry says 1906. No founding or renaming year is printed.

The article's lead says the NAACP began promoting the hymn as the 'Negro national anthem' in 1917, its body says 1919; no year is printed. The entry's 'first recited 1900; set to music 1905' agrees with the article.

The article says construction continued after the French withdrawal and was completed only in 1812 (152 works, 648 cannon); the entry dates the building to 1809-1810, so the later work and the final figures are left out and only the state of October 1810 is given.

The article's lead says the accord was 'concluded' on 15 November 1946; the body says the draft was initialled then and signed in Jakarta on 25 March 1947. The text follows the body, which agrees with the entry.

The entry says the Germans dissolved the Provisional Government in August; the article says the Germans deprived it of its powers and it dissolved itself on 5 August 1941. The text says it lost its authority under German pressure and ended on 5 August without saying who dissolved it. Sužiedėlis's quotation is paraphrased; the article quotes 'political naivite' (sic).

The article dates the documents to the 14th-18th centuries; the entry says fifteenth to eighteenth. I gave no starting century for the documents, only that the Metrica was kept systematically from the second half of the 15th century. Left out the article's alternative claim that Ruthenian prevailed up to the mid-17th century, and the long list of 19th-century editions.
Left out the unsubstantiated 1846 record pike and the cryptozoologist's theory about the afanc.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry
SKIPPED: article under 250 words; beyond the entry it adds only a list of delegates

The article says that in 1843 he 'captured the port of Saint-Louis', which was already the French capital of Senegal; I left the capture out and kept only the trading companies' administration. Left out the treaty negotiations at Grand-Bassam and Assinie and the founding of Libreville (in the entry, not in the article).
The article dates the bombing to 5 October 1944 but elsewhere speaks of the 'air raid 1945' when discussing the white exterior paint; I gave only the 1944 date and left out the paint dispute.
Left out the 1232 massacre of the Lý family, whose authenticity Ngô Sĩ Liên himself doubted. The article gives her age at death as 61, which does not square with 1218-1278; I left the age out.
Left out the article's date of 1884 for Bolivia's loss of its coast in the War of the Pacific, and the Panama Canal comparison.
The article's sentence after Henry II's 1157 campaign ('Even so, he retained the lordships of Oswestry and Whittington') is unclear about who retained them; left out.
Left out the 'Grand History of the Celts' claims about his wives, which come from a book of folklore.
The entry dates the Rathore takeover to around 1400; the article gives no year, only Rao Chunda's reign (c. 1383-1424) and the dowry. I gave no year.
The article gives his birth as March 1707 (and says he was 72 at his marriage in 1779); the entry's dates are 1704-1782. I left out the birth year and his age at marriage.

The article says he studied at the International School of American Archaeology and Ethnology, 'established in 1911', but also that Nuttall sent him to Boas in 1909; I named his teachers without the school or its date.
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, little beyond the entry (area, the Tembe kingdom in two sentences, annexation of Tongaland in 1895)

The article lists Halland among the provinces ceded in its lead, but in the treaty section says Denmark gave up 'its claims to Halland under the Second Treaty of Brömsebro'; I followed the lead's list, which also matches the entry's wording of large territories ceded. Swedish army size on the ice varies by source in the article (6,000-7,000 or up to 12,000); both given and attributed.
The article gives his birth as c. 1794, or 29 August 1790 or 26 May 1794 by different historians; the entry says 1794. I gave no birth date.

The article gives conflicting birth dates (7 July 1807 by his own account, 4 July 1807 by his baptismal certificate, 7 July 1808 in other sources); the entry says 1807. I gave no date of birth. The article says Rancho Petaluma was granted by Governor Figueroa in 1834 and also that he transferred mission land into it; I kept the secularization wording general.

The article gives his dates as c. 1534-1575 but tells of his death in Limahong's attack of 1574; the entry says d. 1574. I gave no birth or death year beyond the 1574 attack. The article says the expedition to Manila was ordered in 1569 'from his base in Mexico City'; left out as unclear. The Battle of Bangkusay (in the entry) is not in the article.
The article dates Masuna fl. c. 508-535 and the Vandalic War to 533; the entry gives only the 508 inscription and the 535 campaign, so no year of the Vandalic War is given beyond 'the 530s'.

The article gives his name as Léonard Mathurin Duphot. It calls the riot one caused by a festival at Joseph's palace; the entry places it outside the French embassy: the text speaks only of a riot, without placing it. The article says Bonaparte used the pretext; the entry says the Directory occupied Rome under Berthier: the text gives no actor for the occupation.

The entry dates his removal and exile to 1623; the article dates the banishment to 1622 (and the poisoning attempt to 1622). The text gives no year for the banishment and none for the poisoning. The entry says he fought at the siege of Osaka in 1615; the article has him in the Winter Campaign and the next year's Summer Campaign without years, so none are given.

The article says that Emperor Maurice abolished Mauretania Sitifensis in 585 by merging it with Mauretania Caesariensis into Mauretania Prima; the entry dates the province to the 7th century and has it absorbed in the Arab conquest. The merger is left out. The article also dates Gennadius's appointment to 578 while placing the creation of the exarchate in 585.

The article's lead says he was king from 1872; its Early life section, like the entry, says he became king in 1875. No year of accession is given. The article gives the Swazi force against Sekhukhune as 10,000 in one place and his army as more than 15,000 in another: no figure is given. The article spells the adviser both 'Offy Sherpstone' and 'Offy' Shepstone.
The article gives his death as 27 November 1984 in the lead and 28 November 1984 in the body; the text says only November 1984.
The article's History section mentions a source attributing the Welsh words to Ceiriog in 1890, which it calls clearly predated; left out.

The article gives both 'more than 70' and 'seventy-one' Wajin killed; the entry says about seventy. No total is given in the text. The entry's note that the shogunate then took a closer interest in Ezo is not in the article.

The article dates his reign 1860-1884 and his westward conquests to the 1860s; the entry places the building of his state and his conquests in the 1870s and his war with Unyanyembe in 1871-1875. No decade is given for his accession or conquests. The article calls his state the largest by area in 19th-century East Africa; left out as a ranking.
The article spells the leader both Tenamaztle and Tenamzaztle; the text uses Tenamaztle.

The entry dates his turn against Harumoto to 1549 and has him defeat Harumoto at Eguchi; the article dates the rebellion to 28 October 1548 and says he defeated Miyoshi Masanaga at Eguchi in 1549. Neither the year of the rebellion nor the battle is given. The article gives his death as 10 August 1564 in the lead and 4 July 1564 in the body (probably the lunar date); only the year is given. The article calls the brother who was executed both Ataka and Atagi Fuyuyasu, and the brother killed at Kumeda both Miyoshi Saneyasu and Miyoshi Yoshikata.

The entry calls her a respected clan matron. The article reports a dispute: she has been called 'head of the Six Nations matrons', but Robert Allen finds no evidence she was ever a clan matron, while Feister and Pulis say she became one of the Mohawk matrons. Left out of the text. The article gives the land Johnson left her as 25,000 acres in one section and 15,000 in another; no figure is given.

The entry dates Eulogius's visit to around 848; the article says only that he wrote about the monastery in 852. The text gives the letter of 852 and no date for the visit. The article's legend of the Holy Grail found in the church wall is left out.

The entry calls their language Adamawa and speaks of their resistance to the emirate of Muri; the article mentions neither, so the text adds no history. The article's claims that they are the largest group of Taraba State and the second largest of the Middle Benue are left out.

The article dates his birth c. 845/6 from al-Dhahabi's age of 90; the entry gives c. 845. Neither year is given in the text, only the age. The article speaks of a 'second Fatimid army' in 920-922; the entry and lead say 920. Not repeated.
The article dates his death to 27 May 398; the text says early summer 398 only.
The Book of Jin's description of his height is left out.

The article dates the defeat of Farhat-ul-Mulk to 1391 (Kamboi) and 1392 (Kambor) in two accounts; no year is given. The article's lead gives his rule as 1391-1403 and 1404-1411 and his death as 10 January 1411; the entry says only d. 1411 and has him take the title of sultan around 1407, which the text follows.

The article dates the Ottoman annexation of Vlorë and Berat to 1415-17; the entry gives 1417; no year is given. The article confuses Theodor II and Theodor Corona Musachi in places (the chronicle has Theodor II at Kosovo in 1389, the poetry names Theodor Corona as Marko's enemy).
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (course, tributaries, a shipwreck of 1635, fish species); a longer text would be padded
Arita porcelain, named in the entry, is not in the article; left out. The article's line on the present head of the foundation ('As of 2026') left out under the present-day rule.

The entry dates the movement 11th–18th century; the article says 11th to 19th centuries (with the final annexation of Champa in 1832). The overall span is not stated in the text; 1832 is told as the annexation of the remnant. Human Rights Watch's criticism of the present government left out under the present-day rule.

The article puts the mass emigration to Lithuania right after the treaty of 1281; the entry says the Semigallians held out for several years and withdrew to Lithuania when resistance collapsed in 1290. The text says only 'later' and gives no date for the emigration. The article spells the place Kernave; written Kernavė here if the checker accepts it.
The entry says Thihathu murdered him at Prome; the article says he was captured on the way from Hlegya to Pagan and does not name the place of death. The text gives no place.
The article does not give the year of dissolution (only after the Velvet Revolution); the entry's 1990 is not repeated.
Present-day statements (current ruling party, current office bearers 'as of November 2026') left out. Records of votes and preferential votes left out as rankings.
The entry gives some 26,000 dead by common estimate; the article says roughly 27,000. No figure given in the text.
The entry speaks of the remains of dozens of people; the article says at least 100 skeletons. No count given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the entry (the Roman conquest, Via Flavia, abandonment in the 6th century)
The Licchavi, Thakuri and Malla kings named in the entry are not in the article. The quotation on Newar Buddhism being in retreat before Theravada left out as a present-day judgement.

The article's excerpt does not cover the reign itself (Mandlakazi, Coolela), so the text says nothing of it beyond the succession. The article gives Mzila's reign as 1861–1884 in one place and 1862–1884 in its table; no start year printed.

The entry says he had himself appointed governor in 1558; the article says he took over the province in 1558 after defeating the Mạc commander. The text gives 1558 only for the taking of the province, which fits both.

The article also cites the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as having Sihtric Cáech kill his brother Niall in 921; left out, as the entry dates Niall's death to 919. The article writes longfort; written longphort here, the usual form, if the checker accepts it. The O'Neill surname named in the entry is not in the article.

The article gives the birth year as 1288 without 'c.'; the entry has c. 1288. Not given in the text. The entry's statement that his descendants ruled the combined duchy until 1521 is not in the article. The article spells Ratibór; Racibórz used as in the entry and in the article's marriage section.

The LAMCO iron mining on the Liberian side from 1963, named in the entry, is not in the article. The History section carries the ecology for want of historical material; the article has nothing on human history beyond the reserve.

The entry says the site was first excavated by Kozlov's expedition in 1924–1925; the article says Ballod excavated one mound in 1913. The text says only that Ballod came upon the site and sent finds, and that Kozlov opened eight mounds, without calling either the first excavation. Töv is spelt Tov in the article.
The entry spells the client king Togidubnus; the article Cogidubnus. Both are forms of the same name; the text uses the article's full form.
The capture by Congo Free State forces in 1893, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The article gives the height as 33 m in its lead and 30 m later, and the building time as six months (25 January to 26 June 1702) in one place and fewer than five months in 1701–1702 in another; neither figure printed. The lead says the deity is not known to the public, while a later section names Siddhi Lakshmi; the text hedges ('is held to be').

The article says King Edward II granted Thomond to Thomas de Clare in 1276, which cannot be right for that year (Edward I reigned); the king is not named. The article dates the end of the kingdom variously to 1542 and the surrender to 1543; only 1543 for the arms is printed, matching the entry's 1543.
The article dates the battle and his death 498/496 BCE; the entry gives c. 496 BCE, so no year is printed for the battle.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words; beyond the entry it adds only a few lines on later broadcasts and sporting ceremonies

The article does not say when the family settled at Donegal Castle; it names Red Hugh O'Donnell I (reigned c. 1460-1505) as its builder. The entry's 1474 is not repeated. Present-day chiefs and clan officers left out.
The article gives his death as 7 February 1538 in the lead and 6 February 1538 in the text; only February 1538 is printed.
SKIPPED: article of about 250 words; beyond the entry it lists only a few works of art inside, too little for three sections

The article has Simeon die in 1470 and Kiev then made a voivodeship; the entry says the family ruled Kiev until 1471 (the voivodeship was formed in 1471). No year printed for the change. The article does not give the date the male line died out; the entry's 1592 is not repeated. The article's 'Simeon moved his court from Kapyl to Slutsk' and 'Simeon ... near Babruysk in 1502' cannot be the Simeon who died in 1470; both are left without a name, and the 1502 battle is left out.
The article gives his birth as 1554 yet says he was believed to be 90-100 in 1646; no birth year is printed.

The entry says the opera closed in 1738; the article has Telemann's management ending in 1738 and the building used by Mingotti's Italian troupe from 1743 to 1750. Written as the end of the German company, the later use told separately.
The article dates his satrapy c. 530-520 BCE and counts Darius among the kings he served; the entry names Cyrus and Cambyses only. No dates printed.
The article gives no years for his headship of the Self-Administration; the entry's 1942-1945 is not repeated.

The entry names Maharero for the 1863 fighting; the article names Andersson and the Herero against Christian Afrikaner at the battle and has Maharero elected commander in the 1860s. Both are compatible; Maharero not repeated.

The November 2026 dividend dispute and the corruption allegations against named former ministers are left out (ongoing; living people). Production forecasts and the GDP share are left out as projections.
SKIPPED: article of about 300 words, mostly tourism and fauna; beyond the entry it adds only the builder's name and the lake's area
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, mostly lists of municipalities; its history is three sentences, less than the entry
The entry says he handed his rights to Venice in 1503; the article does not mention this, only his failed attack on Rimini that year. Not contradicted, not repeated.

The article gives the Nguyễn attack on Kauthara two ways (a Cham attack on Phu Yen in 1611 with Kauthara lost in 1653, and a Nguyễn annexation of Kauthara in 1611); both left out. The article also says Panduranga stood until the late 17th century; the entry's final annexation in 1832 is consistent with the article's capital at Phan Rí Cửa until 1832, but the annexation itself is not told. Po Sri Agarang reign given as the article gives it, 1195 or 1205.
The article tells the story without naming the Shiji; it is introduced as the traditional account, as the entry attributes it to the Shiji.

The article calls Somare prime minister from 1972; the entry says he became the first prime minister. Kept to 'led the government'. Left out the 'as of 2023 largest party' line and the attribution of the PNC defections to O'Neill's leadership crisis.

SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, most of it already in the entry (walls, palaces, bronzes like Zhengzhou, copper); too little to add. Note: the article says discovered 1954 and excavated in 1974 and 1976, the entry says excavated from the 1950s.
Date of the killing left out: the entry says around 1285 and the article's lead gives 1285, but its Life section says probably between February 1283 and 1284.

The article gives c. 1140 and 1140 for his accession in Dakkhinadesa; used 1140 as in its lead. Left out the seizure of the Sacred Relics in 1157, as the article does not make clear which side took them.
Date of the Pandya conquest left out: the entry says around 920, while the article has Madurai taken by his third regnal year and the decisive battle at Vellur around 915.
Kept the dating debate as the article gives it; the entry's c. 650 and 'generally dated to the 7th century' agree with the mid-7th-century view most scholars hold.
The article dates both of Stein's visits to 1892 (a slip); wrote 'a later visit'. It gives Lalitaditya as (695–731 CE), unclear whether life or reign; left out.
The article dates one Laufen foundation to 1618, before he became archbishop in 1619; the foundation years were left out.
Left out membership figures given 'as of 2025', current seat counts and the 2026 Tobago House of Assembly result.
Internal self-government left undated: the article's overview says 1964, its body says 1 January 1963. Left out the 'Today' section's claims about corruption and present scepticism.
The article's wartime sections are confused in places (it says he first travelled in the Middle East aged 25, and mixes Curzon and Nixon); only clear facts were used.
Founding date left out: the entry says 6th century BCE, the article's lead says 7th or 6th century BC and its etymology section probably the beginning of the 6th.
The article spells the governor Arysandes, the entry Aryandes; the name was left out. The article spells her Pheretima; the entry's Pheretime is used.
